title: Candles in Leipzig (1989)
hook: Monday prayers for peace in St. Nicholas Church become peaceful marches with candles, and soon the Wall is open

segments.voice: Yesterday, icon, an icon on a corner shelf and a prayer whispered on a grandmother's knee. Your line was the babushkas kept it. Who did you thank? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

Monday evening in the East German city of Leipzig. Outside St. Nicholas Church, a sign says the church is open to all. Inside, the pews fill. Some people come every week to pray for peace. Some haven't been inside a church in their lives, and come because it's one of the few rooms in town where people say out loud what they think. A pastor reads, people pray, someone speaks about the country. Then the doors open, and the crowd steps out into the dark square, and many of them are holding lit candles. Today, a city that walked with candles.

East Germany was a communist state that watched its people closely. The churches were tolerated, barely, and they became a kind of shelter for honest talk. In Leipzig, St. Nicholas held prayers for peace every Monday, and its pastor, Christian Führer, kept the doors open to anyone: believers, doubters, people who wanted to leave the country, people who wanted to change it. Church peace groups wore a badge with a picture of a man beating a sword into a plow, a line found in the prophets Isaiah and Micah. In the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks." Then the prayers spilled into the streets. After the service, people walked the ring road around the city center, more of them as the weeks went on, holding candles and calling out: no violence, and, we are the people. Here's the detail people in Leipzig tell. If you carry a candle in the open air, you need one hand to hold it and the other to shield the flame. That leaves no hand free for a stone. On one Monday that autumn, soldiers and police were ready, and people feared shooting. It didn't come. Not long after, the Berlin Wall opened. A remark often credited to an East German leader puts it plainly: they were prepared for everything, except candles and prayers. Historians name other causes for the fall: the economy, Moscow's changes, a border opening elsewhere. The prayers weren't the whole story. But they were in it, and Jesus's words were too: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."
screen: `ONE HAND FOR THE CANDLE, ONE TO SHIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle for peace. If you have a candle and can light it safely, do. If not, a phone's light or a lamp will do. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame, or the light, and cup your hands around it, the way they did in Leipzig. Notice that your hands are full. Then bring to mind one place, near or far, where people need peace tonight. A street, a country, a home. Hold it there with the light. If you pray, you can pray for that place. The bell holds the time.
Peacemakers. Leipzig's Monday prayers for peace that became candlelit marches with no violence, part of how the wall came down.
Your line: candles and prayers. Today, when something makes you want to pick up a stone, even a verbal one, keep your hands full of something else. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: St. Nicholas Church in Leipzig still holds Monday prayers for peace. In churches of several traditions, Christians light candles as a sign of prayer, including prayer for peace.

notes: Claims rule: the year (1989) stays in the index title and the close screen only; not in the voice. No crowd sizes given.
'Monday, five o'clock' is the traditional time of the Leipzig peace prayers; confirm.
The 'open to all' sign (Nikolaikirche – offen für alle) and Pastor Christian Führer: confirm.
The 'Schwerter zu Pflugscharen' badge of the East German church peace movement is described as 'a man beating a sword into a plow'; confirm.
The candle detail (two hands, none for a stone) is a remark associated with Führer and others; framed as 'the detail people in Leipzig tell'. Confirm.
The remark 'we were prepared for everything, except candles and prayers' is usually attributed to Horst Sindermann; paraphrased and framed as 'often credited to an East German leader'. Confirm.
The decisive Monday (October 9) is described without a date as 'one Monday that autumn'; confirm.
howItsDone: candle-lighting described generally; confirm. Confirm Monday peace prayers continue at the Nikolaikirche.
